The Great Plains. A broad expanse of grassland and prairie stretching from Canada to Texas, between the Rocky Mountains and the Mississippi River. Spanning roughly five hundred thousand square miles across the central United States and southern Canada, the region is characterized by flat or gently rolling terrain, sparse precipitation, and historically vast herds of buffalo and nomadic Native American peoples.

The plains were formed by sediment deposits from ancient glaciers and Rocky Mountain erosion. The elevation gradually decreases eastward from the Rockies to the Mississippi.

Precipitation decreases westward. The eastern portions receive enough rain for corn and wheat, while the western High Plains are semi-arid and suited to ranching.

For millennia, Native American peoples including the Comanche, Cheyenne, Sioux, and Blackfoot hunted buffalo in nomadic bands adapted to grassland life.

The buffalo, or American bison, numbered perhaps thirty to sixty million before European contact. Systematic hunting reduced them to near extinction by 1890, destroying the ecological and cultural foundation of Plains tribes.

Rapid settlement after the Civil War, driven by the Homestead Act of 1862, brought farmers, ranchers, and railroads. The Transcontinental Railroad, completed in 1869, accelerated development.

The Dust Bowl of the nineteen-thirties was caused by drought and soil depletion from decades of intensive farming. It created an ecological and economic catastrophe, forcing mass migration westward.

The plains remain the agricultural core of North America. The region produces corn, wheat, and cattle on an industrial scale.

Climate variability and isolation characterize the region. Winters are harsh, summers hot, and economic cycles tied to commodity prices create boom-and-bust dynamics that have defined the plains experience throughout history.
